conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your hospital doctors. You were admitted because your INR was very high—9.8—which means your blood is too thin and you’re at risk for bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that sounds scary. I didn’t feel any bleeding, though. I just had that sore throat again, like a few months ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you mentioned discomfort when swallowing. That’s likely esophagitis, possibly from yeast, especially since you’ve had it before. We’re going to treat that with an antifungal medication called fluconazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but why did my INR go so high? I stopped my Coumadin when it was 6, like they told me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. Even though you stopped Coumadin four days ago, it can stay in your system. Also, your recent peritoneal dialysis catheter placement and possibly your diet or other meds like amiodarone may have contributed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And now with this fluconazole, will that make it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fluconazole can increase your INR even more. That’s why we’re not restarting Coumadin for now. You’ll stay off it until your INR is back in the safe range—between 2.0 and 3.0.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my transplant meds? I’m on tacrolimus and sirolimus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent point. Fluconazole also affects those levels. We’ll lower your tacrolimus and sirolimus doses starting in two days and check your levels twice a week to keep them safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve also been having some pain in my right hand. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an X-ray this morning. Good news—it shows no fracture or dislocation. But we did see vascular calcifications and some bone thinning, which are common with your history of diabetes and kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So nothing broken. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your morning labs just came back. Your INR has improved—from 9.3 down to 4.6. That’s a good drop after the vitamin K you got during dialysis yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? Is it safe to go back to rehab soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you today. Your heart and lungs are stable, your dialysis access is healing well, and you’re feeling better overall. We’ll send you back to extended care with clear instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do after I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take fluconazole for two weeks for the esophagitis. Hold off on Coumadin. We’ll reduce your tacrolimus and sirolimus soon. And you must get your INR and transplant drug levels checked twice a week while on fluconazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to follow up. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Your nurse will go over the written instructions, and you’ll see your specialist soon to review all your meds. Take care, and keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before discharge. The nurse changed your PD catheter dressing—looks clean and dry. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve been keeping it covered like they told me last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Also, your urine showed some yeast, but the fluconazole will cover that. Just keep an eye out for any new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. You’re alert, walking with your walker, and your vitals are stable. We’re confident you can continue recovering at the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: no Coumadin, take fluconazole daily, and get those blood tests twice a week. Your care team will coordinate the rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve got it written down. I’ll follow through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
